messages.subject: Wanted: proof-readers !
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

right now, Andy Royle and I are finishing the writing of the 2nd volume of the Applied Hierarchical Modeling for Ecologists book project (i.e., AHM2).  Academic Press tell us that they will send us the proofs startin in the last week of August.

Now, we are looking for 1-3 additional proof-readers for each of the 12 chapters which are listed here:

12. Relative-abundance models for population dynamics
13. Modeling population dynamics while accounting for imperfect detection
14. Hierarchical models of survival
15. Modeling species distribution and range dynamics using dynamic occupancy models
16. Modeling metacommunity dynamics using dynamic community models
17. Multi-state occupancy models
18. Modeling false-positives
19. Models for species interactions
20. Spatial modeling for abundance and occupancy
21. Integrated models
22. Spatial distance sampling and spatial capture-recapture (SCR)
23. Conclusions

If you're interested in helping us and and could do the proofs for one or more chapters, please let us know. We would expect you to give a chapter one thorough read and return to us within 1 week from receipt any detected errors or serious awkwardnesses in the text.

The audience of this mail is not limited to the two Google groups to which it is sent, so if you like you can also forward to colleagues who you think might be interested.

Thank you very much.

Best regards  --- Marc & Andy

messages.subject: total covariate effect in zero-inflated/hurdle models
messages.subject_clean: total covariate effect in zero-inflated/hurdle models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am fitting some zero-inflated count models where both the zero-inflation probability (psi) and the mean for the counts (lam) are functions of the same covariate. So, something like this:
logit(psi) = a_psi _b_psi * X
log(lam) = a_lam + b_lam * X
Now I am interested in the total effect of X on Y (Y being my zero-inflated counts). Is there a way to calculate that from estimates of b_psi and b_lam?
A quick google search showed that there are marginalized versions of these models that directly estimate the total effect of X on the mean of the zero-inflated counts. But I'd like to know if there is a way to determine this effect using estimates from the regular ZIP model. And, if there is a way to do so, how does that change if you have a hurdle model rather than a ZIP model.
Any thoughts much appreciated!
Thanks
Rahel

Dear Rahel,

I don't really have an answer for this, but I wonder about the estimability of such a model: unless you have replicates in the second stage of the model (for log(lam)), intuitively I feel that estimability depends exclusively on the fact that you have a logit for the first stage and a log for the second. I wonder how stable the inferences from such a model are likely to be ?

Best regards  ---- Marc

Hi Marc,
we actually do have replication on the count level. This is a situation where there is (ecologically) no way around including the covariate on both model levels. I do realize didn't phrase my post very well, though; I am fitting a hurdle model, so that I'm not trying to separate out structural from count zeros, just modeling the two components separately (and there is no way around that for the sake of model fit).
Best
Rahel

messages.subject: Coping with violation of closure assumption
messages.subject_clean: Coping with violation of closure assumption
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am seeking a bit of guidance and reassurance. I am new to mixture models and Bayesian analysis in general, so I apologise if these seem like very basic questions, or I am misunderstanding stuff.

Background; I am working on a community N-mixture model, borrowing heavily from Chapter 11 of Kery & Royle. I have repeat point count bird data from 190 sites, divided between 18 transects (9 - 12 points per transect). I revisited each point 8 times in the course of a year. Points were >400m apart, so there was no double counting in the course of a single survey, but birds almost certainly moved among points between surveys. (Mean time between surveys was 25 days). The surveys were split 4 - 4 between two seasons, and migratory birds were only present in the first season.

I propose to include a gamma parameter for season, to cope with the migratory species. However, I am concerned about violating the closure assumption within-season as well. I think it is probably ok to assume closure between transects as they are mostly well separated. However, between points seems like too much of an ask. In Chapter 6 of Kery & Royle they have a short section on multiscale models, incorporating a random effect of 'region'. Would it be reasonable for me to incorporate 'transect' in this way? And would that be enough to cope with the fact that the points are open?

Am I making any glaring errors? Any thoughts people may have would be really appreciated.

Kind regards,
Tom

messages.subject: Year trend estimate - Sollmann et al. 2015
messages.subject_clean: Year trend estimate - Sollmann et al. 2015
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I've been using the JAGS code from Sollman et al.'s 2015 open-population distance sampling paper (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/14-1625.1) and I have a question about the code for trend. Mainly I've used the explaination on pages 518-520 of the AHM book to make my own version of the "Independence Model", which is just a simple linear trend in abundance across years. The process model part of the code looks like this: log(lambda[s,t]) <- beta0 + beta1*chap[s] + beta2*(t - t/2) where lambda is abundance at site s during year t.

I get that beta2 is the trend in abundance through time, but why use beta2*(t - t/2)? Why not just use beta2*t? It seems like the t - t/2 is mainly a way to make the index of year a smaller number in the model and possibly a way to get quicker convergence, similar to how you typically standardize your covariates to have a mean of 0 and SD of 1. So if you have a range of t indexes from 1 to 50 they range from 0.5 to 25 in the model. Am I correct in assuming this? Or is there some other reason that I'm missing? I've attached the code from the AHM book for reference.

Thanks for the help.

-Jerry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jerry,

There could well be a motivation I’m missing, but looks to me like this is centering the temporal periods, which maybe makes it a little easier to think about the marginal effects of other covariates if a trend exists—N at t=0 with a centered time effect is more like an average N than an N at the beginning of the time series.

John
